title: Product Owner
summary: Co-founded an EdTech SaaS that automated STEM exam grading using computer vision, OCR, and NLP; as the only engineer, designed and shipped the entire platform — Django app, AWS infrastructure, and a 10-stage automated grading pipeline.
description:
AidProf was an early-stage SaaS startup targeting educational institutions in Chile and Latin America. The product let teachers upload scanned student exams and receive automated, annotated feedback reports, gradebooks, and performance analytics — combining computer vision, OCR, and NLP to interpret handwritten math and text responses against teacher-defined rubrics.

Official title was Product Owner, chosen intentionally to signal to investors that the product was driven by both engineering and a deep understanding of business logic. In practice the role was solo full-stack developer, data engineer, ML engineer, DevOps engineer, and product manager — ~90% of the codebase was written single-handedly.

**Full-stack ownership.** Owned the entire stack end-to-end: the Django web application (auth, multi-institution data model, rubric builder, bulk PDF upload, review dashboard, analytics, grade predictions), the AWS infrastructure (EC2 with nginx + gunicorn, S3, RDS MySQL, Lambda prototypes, IAM), the CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions deploying to a single production environment), and a separate WordPress marketing site.

**Automated grading pipeline.** The technical centerpiece was the automated grading pipeline: PDFs were rasterized via pdf2image + Poppler, ROIs (answer boxes) were detected with OpenCV using Gaussian blur, inverse binary thresholding, and contour hierarchy filtering, then labelled interactively by the teacher. Each ROI was base64-encoded and POSTed to the Mathpix /v3/latex endpoint for handwritten math OCR (chosen after benchmarking AWS Textract via Lambda). Rubric and student LaTeX strings were vectorized with CountVectorizer and compared via cosine similarity, with bucketed thresholds surfacing borderline cases for manual review. Results were pivoted into a multi-index DataFrame, mapped onto Chile's 1–7 grading scale, and exported as styled .xlsx files via openpyxl. Matplotlib generated donut, bar/box, and histogram charts; PIL overlaid ✓/✗ icons and scores on student page images to produce per-student feedback PDFs.

**Key technical decisions.** Product decisions reflected the startup constraints: Django server-rendered templates over an SPA for delivery speed; bag-of-words + cosine similarity over a fine-tuned model because there wasn't enough data yet; rubric-defined-in-UI as the design choice that made automated grading possible at all — capturing scoring weights, data types, expected answers, and key sections upfront gave the system everything it needed to grade without further annotation.

**Outcome & go-to-market.** The product was demoed to 3 colleges and 5 independent teachers with consistent positive feedback. The startup concluded in February 2022 not because the technology failed but because of go-to-market resistance: B2C buyers (teachers) wouldn't pay out-of-pocket for institutional tooling, and B2B buyers (institutions) had functioning manual workflows with switching costs that overrode the demonstrated time savings.
impact: Sole technical co-founder on a 3-person team; wrote ~90% of the codebase across product, infrastructure, and ML pipeline
Designed and shipped a 10-stage automated grading pipeline (PDF → image → OCR → NLP comparison → annotated feedback PDFs + gradebook + analytics charts)
Built the full Django SaaS platform from scratch: auth, multi-institution data model, rubric builder, bulk upload, review dashboard, per-student analytics, and linear-regression grade predictions
Architected and operated full AWS infrastructure (EC2 + nginx/gunicorn, S3, RDS MySQL, Lambda, IAM) with GitHub Actions CI/CD to production
Integrated Mathpix /v3/latex OCR API after benchmarking against AWS Textract for superior handwritten-math accuracy
Demoed the live product to 3 colleges and 5 independent teachers with consistent positive validation on automation and time savings
Navigated two go-to-market pivots (B2C → B2B) and presented to investors as the technical co-founder

title: Data Engineer
summary: Data Engineer at a 90-person AI-powered EdTech SaaS (FT Fastest Growing 2023, ISO 27001) serving 30+ higher-education institutions across 3 continents — owned ETL/ELT pipelines, all D2L Brightspace LMS integrations across 5 international clients, the Pentaho → Azure Synapse migration, and a Streamlit internal platform with 20+ tools.
description:
uPlanner is an AI-powered B2B SaaS for higher education (founded 2012, HQ Miami, 90+ specialists, offices across 8 countries). It serves 30+ institutions including Universidad de los Andes, PUC Chile, and Aliat Universities Mexico — at scale, 20 Peruvian public universities simultaneously covering 350,000 students. The company was named one of the Americas' Fastest Growing Companies by the Financial Times in 2023 and holds ISO/IEC 27001 certification. Products span the full institutional lifecycle: uForecast (demand), uPlanning (scheduling), uBooking (events), uAssessment (curriculum), uEngagement (retention), uClass (attendance/grades), uExperience (mobile app), and uSuite (integrated platform). Solutions are frequently customized per client — every product can vary in implementation detail, so engineers must maintain deep awareness of client-specific configurations across multiple simultaneous deployments.

As a Data Engineer on the Data Services team (3–6 people, fully remote), responsibilities spanned the full lifecycle of data pipelines: design, development, maintenance, documentation, and client-facing support. Operated simultaneously as a pipeline developer, integration engineer, cloud-migration contributor, internal-tooling builder, and technical representative in international client meetings. Carried significant autonomy — owning end-to-end integrations, leading client meetings, and independently driving projects from requirements through delivery.

**ETL/ELT pipeline ownership.** The core ETL system was built on Pentaho Data Integration, organized into 6 sequential steps per client per run (SFTP file discovery → format validation → staging load to MariaDB → cross-referencing into product DB → algorithm execution → report generation, plus a MongoDB key-value step for mobile data). Python scripts were layered throughout the pipeline to handle client-specific transformations, validations, and business logic across multiple simultaneous deployments.

**D2L Brightspace LMS integration suite.** Owned all integrations with D2L Brightspace REST API — uPlanner's primary external data source, used across 5 international clients in Colombia, Mexico, Argentina, France, and others. Built grades processing, attendance tracking, course/curriculum fetching, and curriculum upload automation, all following a uPlanner-MySQL → D2L-API → cross-reference → business-logic → output pattern. Handled token-based auth (credentials in DB, access tokens refreshed per session), pagination for endpoints returning tens of thousands of records, and async export-job polling for D2L endpoints that trigger background jobs rather than returning data immediately.

**Curriculum upload automation (Colombia client).** A custom Python integration that fetched uPlanner's generated curricula from MySQL, cross-referenced each against D2L courses via the Brightspace API, and programmatically uploaded curriculum files to D2L as they became ready. Replaced a manual teacher workflow consuming 250+ hours per semester.

**Automated error logging.** Designed and implemented systematic error capture, categorization, and surfacing across ETL transformation and validation stages — reducing diagnostic and resolution time on pipeline issues by 43%.

**Pentaho → Azure Synapse migration.** Initiated as greenfield: designed and built the first complete ETL pipeline from scratch on Synapse to evaluate the tooling, establish development patterns, and measure performance. Used findings to define the migration strategy for legacy pipelines, then began migrating in batches. Synapse components used: Pipelines, Notebooks (Python/PySpark), Spark Pools, SQL Pools, Data Lake storage. Improved integration efficiency by 35%. Migration was underway at time of departure (first new pipeline built; 2 legacy pipelines successfully migrated).

**Internal Streamlit platform.** Designed and developed a Streamlit web platform consolidating 20+ internal tools used across Data Engineering, Product, Customer Success, and Data Science. After two years of repeatedly solving the same categories of CS-reported issues, the recurring query patterns were compiled into purpose-built, form-driven tools — CS staff went from waiting up to 2 hours per issue (no SQL knowledge, blocked on engineer availability) to under 2 minutes via instant self-service. Tools included file transformation/parsing utilities, recurrent DB query runners with friendly UIs, DB job management, environment/client config comparison, and API testing interfaces.

**Data model restructuring.** Led cross-functional meetings with technical, product, and customer service teams to restructure the data model and realign product requirements, identifying misalignments between internal data structure and client onboarding needs. Reduced initial customer data delivery time by 20%.

**Client-facing work.** Served as the technical face of the Data Services team in international client meetings — requirements gathering, feasibility evaluation, project follow-ups, and live-deployment issue resolution. Frequently led meetings directly across Colombia, Mexico, Argentina, France, and other countries.

**Infrastructure & DevOps.** uPlanner runs a multi-tenant database architecture on MySQL where each client is provisioned with isolated development, QA, and production instances — so every pipeline, integration, and tooling change had to be environment-aware and validated against QA before promotion to live institutional data. The team standardized on the Atlassian Suite for the full delivery lifecycle: work was tracked as Jira tickets, version-controlled in Bitbucket, and shipped through Bamboo's automated deployment pipelines across the dev → QA → prod environments.

**Mentorship & documentation.** Mentored 2–3 engineers across the team lifecycle, both during onboarding and as part of formal growth plans. Maintained technical documentation for all owned developments (pipelines, integrations, automations, tools) as a team-wide standard.
impact: Eliminated 250+ hours of manual teacher work per semester for a Colombian university client via curriculum-upload automation against the D2L Brightspace API
Reduced common Customer Success query resolution from up to 2 hours to under 2 minutes via a Streamlit internal platform with 20+ self-service tools
Reduced data-validation and transformation work time by 43% through systematic automated error logging across ETL pipelines
Improved integration efficiency by 35% as part of the Pentaho → Azure Synapse migration (first greenfield pipeline + 2 legacy pipelines migrated at time of departure)
Reduced initial customer data delivery time by 20% by leading a cross-functional data-model restructuring
Owned all D2L Brightspace LMS integrations end-to-end across 5 international clients in Colombia, Mexico, Argentina, France, and others
Mentored 2–3 engineers across onboarding and formal growth plans
Led international client meetings as the technical representative of the Data Services team

title: Computer Science Engineering (Ingeniería Civil Informática)
summary: Six-year professional Computer Science Engineering degree at UAI in Santiago, Chile — closer to a combined Bachelor's plus pre-graduate curriculum than a standard 4-year program, paired with UAI's signature professional-formation pillar (leadership, written/oral expression, critical thinking).
description:
Computer Science Engineering (Ingeniería Civil Informática) at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, Santiago, Chile, ~2014–2020. The degree is a 5-to-6 year professional program — structurally closer to a combined Bachelor's + pre-graduate curriculum than a standard 4-year CS degree — including academic coursework, pre-graduate level courses (equivalent in content to early Master's coursework), and a 6-month professional internship. Final grade: 5.8/7.0 (≈3.4–3.6 GPA on the US 4.0 scale), with specialization years consistently above 6.0 (≈3.7–3.9 GPA, honors-level by US standards).

The path in wasn't a straight line: a strong math background and an engineering household led to a first choice of Chemistry Engineering, then enrollment at UAI in a general engineering program. A required first-year specialization choice — sparked by falling in love with programming through C++ and PHP — made Computer Science the obvious direction. The first couple of years were a genuine shock given the jump in rigor from Chilean high school; once footing was found in the specialization years, performance reflected real engagement.

UAI is known in Chile for producing professionals, not just technicians. Alongside the engineering curriculum, the university runs a structured professional-formation pillar; courses completed included Leadership (multiple), Written Expression, Oral Expression (multiple), Critical Reading, and Argumentation and Critical Thinking — unusual for a CS program, and ultimately the most consequential part of the formation. The most valuable takeaway wasn't technical: it was learning to communicate, express ideas, and lead. Leadership changed the most — across a full semester it dismantled the assumption that clear communication is enough, showing that real leadership requires first understanding what the other person is actually going through, and only then connecting their personal objectives to a shared goal. Communication without empathy is just noise — a quiet foundation for everything that followed.
impact: Graduated with 5.8/7.0 overall (≈3.4–3.6 GPA), specialization years consistently above 6.0 (honors-level by US standards)
Completed UAI's professional-formation pillar — Leadership, Written & Oral Expression, Critical Reading, Argumentation & Critical Thinking — on top of the engineering curriculum
Included a 6-month professional internship as part of the 5-to-6 year program

title: Instructor
summary: Four years (alongside university) at an EdTech company bringing programming, robotics, and innovation courses to schools — grew from instructor to co-owner of an internal teacher-training program, teaching kids across 7 institutions in 2 countries, training 750+ teachers, and doing early product/go-to-market work.
description:
School of Tech (schooloftech.cl) is an educational technology company that brings programming, robotics, and innovation courses to schools and institutions. Joined as an instructor and stayed four years, working up to 30 hours/week alongside university studies (including summers), and grew into considerably more than a classroom teacher. The work spanned three layers.

**Teaching kids (ages 10–18).** Taught programming courses covering video games, electronics, and robotics across 7 educational institutions in 2 countries — from 10-year-olds encountering code for the first time to teenagers building their first electronic projects.

**Training teachers.** Became an instructor for technology tools — Google Docs, Google Sheets, Google Classroom, and collaboration platforms — for 750+ teachers across various establishments, often walking into rooms full of professional educators as a university student and helping them transform how they work.

**Entrepreneurship mentorship.** Mentored 5 teams of Starbucks staff developing technological entrepreneurship projects; one team placed second at the regional level.

**Co-ownership chapter.** After several years of consistent, reliable work, leadership offered a co-ownership role in a new internal project — a program teaching teachers how to transform their practice with technology. This was the first step fully outside the classroom and into something closer to business: conducting statistical analysis of teaching competencies across a dataset of 2,000+ teachers, designing data visualizations to communicate market-research findings, building PowerPoint presentations used directly in sales (showing prospective institutional clients how technology adoption improved outcomes in schools already using the methods), and participating in academic design for teacher-training workshops. In hindsight, this was product thinking and go-to-market work — identifying a market need, quantifying it, and packaging it into a compelling pitch — and the first clear signal of the kind of work that felt closest to the career direction worth pursuing.

The range of audiences was the real education: teaching a 10-year-old robotics, mentoring adults on entrepreneurship, and convincing a room of professional teachers to change how they work each demanded a different register. Over four years and hundreds of classes, that built fluent code-switching between technical depth and accessible simplicity, between authority and humility, between instruction and facilitation.
impact: Taught programming, robotics, and electronics across 7 educational institutions in 2 countries (students aged 10–18)
Trained 750+ teachers on Google Workspace and collaboration tools
Mentored 5 Starbucks staff teams on tech entrepreneurship projects; one placed 2nd at the regional level
As co-owner of an internal teacher-training program, ran statistical analysis across a dataset of 2,000+ teachers and built the data visualizations and sales decks used in go-to-market
Sustained up to 30 hours/week for four years alongside full-time university studies

title: Mentor
summary: Event-based mentor (≈10 events) for high-school students working on personal technology projects — focused on shaping how students think: approaching problems as entrepreneurs, applying critical thinking to new technologies, and moving through innovation circles.
description: Silabuz (no longer in operation as of December 2022) brought in a mentor for a small number of specific events — roughly 10 in total — for high-school students working on personal technology projects, alongside university studies on a freelance, event-based basis. The focus differed from School of Tech: rather than teaching technical skills directly, the role was to shape how students think — how to approach a problem as an entrepreneur rather than just a student, how to apply critical thinking when confronting new technologies, and how to move through innovation circles (brainstorming, discovery, research, validation). Brief and targeted, but it reinforced a lesson already taking shape: teaching methodology and mindset is often more valuable than teaching content.
impact: Mentored high-school students across ≈10 targeted events on entrepreneurial thinking and innovation methodology

title: Event Staff & Waiter
summary: Event-based catering work (0–3 nights/week) for a word-of-mouth private catering company — run simultaneously with engineering studies and teaching. The most unexpectedly formative experience: a lasting, unpretentious respect for people, learned through invisible work done well.
description:
Amelia Izquierdo is a private catering company operating entirely through word-of-mouth referrals. Each shift was an event — a different venue, client, and setup — so no two nights were the same and there was no room for a bad performance; you had one shot. The work covered the full arc of an event, from preparation (dessert tables, kitchen assistance, flowers, table setup) through service (welcoming and attending guests): physical, fast-paced, and entirely people-facing. This ran from 2016 to 2019, several nights a week, simultaneously with studying engineering and teaching kids and teachers at School of Tech — at points all three in parallel.

The experience least expected to be formative turned out to be exactly that. Event catering is unglamorous, invisible work; no one at the table knows or cares about your background. The lasting takeaway wasn't about hustle or stress, though both were tested — it was quieter: no one is only what they appear to be. Everyone has a story, and everyone deserves the chance to prove themselves regardless of the role they're currently playing. That fundamental, unpretentious respect for people didn't come from a course — it came from showing up, doing invisible work, and paying attention.
impact: Worked 0–3 event nights per week for three years while simultaneously studying engineering full-time and teaching at School of Tech

title: Competitive Swimmer & Personal Drive
summary: Nine years as a competitive swimmer through childhood and high school, training alongside future Olympians on a 4:00 AM–8:30 PM daily schedule. The discipline, structure, and proactivity it installed early became the operating system carried into everything since.
description:
Before university, before teaching, before any of the professional story, there was swimming — nine years of competition from childhood through high school. At peak training the daily schedule ran: 4:00 AM wake and breakfast; bike to the club; 2 hours of swimming; bike to school; full school day; bike back to the club; 1 hour of gym; 2 more hours of swimming; bike home; home by 8:30 PM. Saturdays included, for years — training alongside people who went on to compete at the Olympics.

The point of the story isn't to impress; it's the most honest explanation of a working style. That schedule, maintained across childhood and adolescence, built more than fitness — it installed a complete operating system: organized, structured, proactive, someone who doesn't leave for tomorrow what can be done today. Those weren't values adopted later; they were installed early, through repetition and physical consequence, and carried into everything after quitting competitive swimming before university.

Outside structured commitments, the university years went into building a social life and being present for people — showing up for friends, family, and whoever needs something done; reliability as a personal trait, not just a professional one. The people closest would describe a good friend — funny, happy, trustworthy, reliable, honest — and would also name the biggest blind spot: being demanding to a fault with oneself, holding personal performance to a standard that can become personal. It's not perfectionism for its own sake; it's caring too much — the same quality that makes for reliability makes things hard when they fall short.

There was no single moment of conversion into tech; the path assembled itself — a natural aptitude for math and problem-solving from an engineering household, a first university year that made programming click, four years of teaching that proved complexity could be communicated to anyone, a co-ownership role that revealed a pull toward analyzing, building, and solving real problems, and a growing restlessness with pure teaching. The throughline: not someone satisfied operating inside a fixed lane, but someone who wants the full picture — the technical problem, the human need behind it, and the clearest path between the two.
impact: Competed as a swimmer for 9 years, from childhood through high school
Sustained a 4:00 AM–8:30 PM daily training schedule (4 hours swimming + 1 hour gym, Saturdays included) for years
Trained alongside athletes who went on to compete at the Olympics
